topic: Why does your stomach not digest itself?
hook: Your stomach acid can dissolve metal — so what stops it from eating through your own body?
think_question: If scientists could replicate the stomach's protective mucus, what medical problems might it solve?
q1_text: What is the main phenomenon studied when we ask why the stomach does not digest itself?
q1_a: The stomach lining is protected by a thick layer of mucus that neutralises acid.
q1_b: The stomach produces no acid when it is not digesting food.
q1_c: Stomach cells are made of a special acid-proof protein called keratase.
q2_text: Why is understanding the cause-and-effect mechanism more useful than just memorising the answer?
q2_a: Memorised answers are always correct, so mechanisms are unnecessary.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Mechanisms only apply to chemistry, not to biology or physics.
q3_text: If the mucus lining of the stomach were damaged, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The stomach would produce less hydrochloric acid to compensate for the damage.
q3_b: Digestion would slow down because enzymes would have less space to work.
q3_c: Stomach acid could begin to digest the stomach wall, causing ulcers.

topic: What actually happens when you eat food?
hook: Food travels over 9 metres through your body in a journey that takes days. What really happens along the way?
think_question: If we could engineer artificial digestion outside the body, what health conditions might become curable?
q1_text: What is the correct sequence of digestion in the human body?
q1_a: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
q1_b: Mouth, stomach, oesophagus, large intestine, small intestine
q1_c: Oesophagus, mouth, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of digestion more useful than memorising the result?
q2_a: Memorised facts are always accurate and never need updating
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction
q2_c: Results are easier to remember than mechanisms in biology
q3_text: If a person's stomach produced no acid, what would you predict?
q3_a: Food would be digested faster due to reduced friction
q3_b: More nutrients would be absorbed in the large intestine instead
q3_c: Protein digestion would be severely impaired

topic: What is matter really made of?
hook: A single grain of sand contains more atoms than there are grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches. How?
think_question: If atoms are mostly empty space, why can't your hand pass straight through a table?
q1_text: Which best describes what matter is made of at its most fundamental level?
q1_a: Matter is made of tiny particles called atoms and molecules
q1_b: Matter is made of continuous, unbroken fluid that fills all space
q1_c: Matter is made of invisible waves that have no mass
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism more useful than just memorising the result?
q2_a: Mechanisms are shorter to write and easier to remember in exams
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Mechanisms are always visible so they are easier to verify directly
q3_text: If the number of particles in a fixed space were doubled, what would you predict?
q3_a: The particles would slow down and stop moving entirely
q3_b: The particles would merge into one large continuous substance
q3_c: The density of matter would increase and collisions between particles would rise

topic: Chemical reactions happening inside your body
hook: Right now, thousands of chemical reactions are firing inside you — and without them, you'd be dead in seconds.
think_question: If we could speed up or slow down specific body reactions on demand, which disease would you target first?
q1_text: Which chemical process inside your body breaks glucose into energy?
q1_a: Cellular respiration converts glucose into ATP energy
q1_b: Photosynthesis converts glucose into oxygen and water
q1_c: Fermentation converts glucose into starch for storage
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of a reaction more useful than just knowing the result?
q2_a: Because memorised results are always accurate and never need explaining
q2_b: A mechanism reveals cause-and-effect chains and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Because mechanisms are simpler to write down than results
q3_text: What would happen to body reactions if body temperature dropped significantly?
q3_a: Enzyme activity would increase because cold speeds up molecular collisions
q3_b: Chemical reactions would remain unchanged since temperature does not matter
q3_c: Enzyme activity would slow down, reducing the rate of metabolic reactions

topic: How scientists actually measure the universe
hook: How do scientists measure the distance to a star trillions of kilometres away — without ever leaving Earth?
think_question: If our measurement tools could only detect nearby stars, how would our picture of the universe differ?
q1_text: Which tool do scientists use to measure extremely large astronomical distances?
q1_a: Parallax method using Earth's orbit as a baseline
q1_b: Standard rulers calibrated against laboratory laser measurements
q1_c: Direct radar pulses bounced off distant galaxies
q2_text: Why is identifying the underlying mechanism more scientifically useful than memorising a result?
q2_a: Mechanisms are always simpler to remember than numerical results
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Mechanisms replace the need for experimental data entirely
q3_text: If the baseline used for stellar parallax were doubled, what would happen to the measurable distance range?
q3_a: The measurable range would halve because parallax angle decreases
q3_b: The measurable range would stay the same since angle is absolute
q3_c: The measurable range would roughly double as the parallax angle increases

topic: What is electric charge?
hook: Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. The reason why is stranger than you think.
think_question: Could we ever build a device that makes any object electrically charged on command?
q1_text: What is electric charge?
q1_a: A fundamental property of matter that causes electromagnetic force
q1_b: The flow of electrons through a conductor under voltage
q1_c: The energy stored in a magnetic field around a wire
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism behind electric charge useful?
q2_a: It helps memorise the SI unit of charge (coulomb) faster
q2_b: It reveals the cause-and-effect chain and enables prediction
q2_c: It allows students to skip mathematical derivations entirely
q3_text: If you doubled the electric charge on two nearby particles, what happens to the force between them?
q3_a: The force doubles because charge and force are always proportional
q3_b: The force halves because the field lines spread over a larger area
q3_c: The force quadruples because Coulomb's law depends on the product of charges

topic: How does the human nose actually work?
hook: You can detect over a trillion different smells, yet your nose has fewer receptor types than your eyes. How?
think_question: If artificial noses could diagnose diseases by smell, which illness would be most life-saving to detect this way?
q1_text: What is the primary role of the olfactory receptors in the nose?
q1_a: Olfactory receptor cells detect chemical molecules in the air and send signals to the brain.
q1_b: Olfactory receptors filter dust particles before air enters the lungs.
q1_c: Olfactory receptors warm and humidify incoming air to protect the throat.
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of smell more useful than just knowing that the nose detects odours?
q2_a: Knowing odours exist is enough; the mechanism adds no practical value.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: The mechanism of smell is too complex to be studied at Class 7 level.
q3_text: If the olfactory nerve were blocked, what would you predict would happen to a person's sense of smell?
q3_a: The person would smell more strongly because signals would build up in the receptors.
q3_b: The nose would produce more mucus to compensate for the missing nerve signals.
q3_c: The person would lose the sense of smell because signals could not reach the brain.

topic: The microscopic battle between bacteria and antibiotics
hook: Bacteria have been evolving for 3.8 billion years. Your antibiotic has existed for 80. Who's winning?
think_question: If all antibiotics stopped working tomorrow, how would medicine have to fundamentally change?
q1_text: How do antibiotics kill or stop bacteria?
q1_a: They target bacterial cell structures that human cells do not have
q1_b: They heat the bloodstream to kill bacteria through thermal shock
q1_c: They remove oxygen from tissues so bacteria cannot respire
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of antibiotic resistance important?
q2_a: It helps doctors memorise drug names more easily
q2_b: Knowing the mechanism helps predict and prevent resistance spreading
q2_c: Mechanisms are only useful for chemistry, not biology
q3_text: If antibiotics are overused, what would you predict about bacteria?
q3_a: Bacteria would become larger and easier to detect under microscopes
q3_b: Bacteria would lose their ability to reproduce as quickly
q3_c: Resistant bacteria would survive and multiply, making treatment harder

topic: Why do particles move even when you can't see them?
hook: The atoms in your coffee cup are vibrating at hundreds of metres per second — even when the coffee is cold.
think_question: At absolute zero, particle motion nearly stops. What would a material at absolute zero actually look and feel like?
q1_text: What is the main reason particles in matter are always in motion?
q1_a: Particles possess kinetic energy and move continuously at all temperatures above absolute zero
q1_b: Particles are pushed by gravity which keeps them vibrating constantly
q1_c: Particles move only when an external force such as wind acts on them
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of particle motion more useful than just knowing they move?
q2_a: It saves time because you only need to learn one fact about motion
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Mechanisms are easier to draw in diagrams than descriptions of motion
q3_text: If temperature were lowered toward absolute zero, what would happen to particle motion?
q3_a: Particle motion would increase because cold particles vibrate more rapidly
q3_b: Particle motion would stay constant because temperature does not affect speed
q3_c: Particle motion would approach zero as thermal energy is removed from the system

topic: How do we know a chemical reaction occurred?
hook: A rusting nail, a burning candle, a baking cake — they look nothing alike, yet they're all the same type of event.
think_question: If you could design a chemical reaction that had no visible signs at all, what would you use it for?
q1_text: Which observation is a reliable sign that a chemical reaction has occurred?
q1_a: A new substance is formed with different properties than the reactants
q1_b: The mixture changes its container shape but stays the same substance
q1_c: The colour of the container changes but the chemicals remain the same
q2_text: Why does identifying the mechanism of a reaction matter more than memorising the result?
q2_a: Because results are impossible to verify without laboratory equipment
q2_b: Understanding mechanism lets you predict outcomes in unfamiliar situations
q2_c: Because the mechanism is always more colourful and easy to observe
q3_text: What would happen to observable signs of reaction if you removed heat from an exothermic reaction?
q3_a: The reaction would speed up because less energy is wasted
q3_b: The reaction signs would remain unchanged as heat is not a reactant
q3_c: The reaction rate would slow and temperature rise would be smaller

topic: Why dimensions and units matter
hook: A $327 million Mars orbiter was lost because engineers mixed up metres and feet. Could one wrong unit really do that?
think_question: If every country used completely different measurement systems, how would global science and engineering function?
q1_text: What does dimensional analysis allow a scientist to check about an equation?
q1_a: Whether both sides have the same physical dimensions
q1_b: Whether the numerical coefficients are correct
q1_c: Whether the variables are measured with SI instruments
q2_text: Why is using consistent units more useful than simply knowing a formula by heart?
q2_a: Consistent units eliminate the need for significant figures
q2_b: Consistent units allow the cause-and-effect chain to be traced and errors to be predicted
q2_c: Consistent units make all physical constants equal to one
q3_text: If a physicist switches from metres to centimetres in one term of an equation but not others, what is the likely outcome?
q3_a: The answer will be correct because values are proportional
q3_b: Only the units of the final answer will change, not the numerical value
q3_c: The equation becomes dimensionally inconsistent, producing an incorrect result

topic: How electric fields actually work
hook: Electric fields push charged objects without touching them. What invisible structure in space is doing the pushing?
think_question: If you could map an electric field like a topographic map, what would the landscape around a lightning bolt look like?
q1_text: What does an electric field represent around a charged object?
q1_a: The region where another charge would experience an electric force
q1_b: The path that electrons physically travel between two terminals
q1_c: The potential energy stored inside the charged object itself
q2_text: Why is understanding the electric field mechanism more useful than memorising field values?
q2_a: Mechanism values are always simpler to calculate than field formulas
q2_b: Knowing the mechanism lets you predict field behaviour in new geometries
q2_c: Memorising values is unnecessary once the unit of field (V/m) is known
q3_text: If you moved a test charge twice as far from a point charge, what would happen to the electric field strength?
q3_a: It would halve because the field is inversely proportional to distance
q3_b: It would remain the same because field lines are infinite in extent
q3_c: It would decrease to one-quarter because field strength falls as 1/r squared

topic: Why do we breathe faster after running?
hook: Sprint 100 metres and your breathing doubles within seconds. Your brain detected a change before you even noticed.
think_question: Elite free-divers hold their breath for 20+ minutes. What does that reveal about the limits of conscious breathing control?
q1_text: What is the main reason we breathe faster after running?
q1_a: Muscles use more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide during exercise, so breathing rate increases to meet demand.
q1_b: Running heats the lungs, which makes the diaphragm contract more rapidly automatically.
q1_c: The body needs to cool down quickly, so it exhales hot air faster.
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of increased breathing rate more useful than memorising that we breathe faster?
q2_a: The mechanism is only useful for doctors, not for students.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Memorising the fact is sufficient because breathing rate never changes.
q3_text: If a person held their breath after sprinting, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The muscles would stop producing carbon dioxide to prevent overload.
q3_b: The heart would slow down to reduce the demand for oxygen.
q3_c: Carbon dioxide levels in the blood would rise rapidly, triggering an urgent urge to breathe.

topic: How does your immune system recognize an enemy?
hook: Your immune system builds a memory that can outlast your lifetime — and it learns without a single lesson.
think_question: If we could teach the immune system to recognise cancer cells the way it recognises viruses, what would change?
q1_text: What does the immune system use to identify foreign invaders?
q1_a: Antigens on the surface of pathogens trigger immune recognition
q1_b: The colour of pathogens is detected by white blood cells
q1_c: Body temperature rises and burns pathogens before recognition
q2_text: Why is understanding the immune recognition mechanism useful?
q2_a: It allows doctors to memorise the names of all pathogens
q2_b: It explains how vaccines and immunity work, enabling predictions
q2_c: Immune mechanisms only apply to bacterial infections, not viruses
q3_text: If a person encountered a pathogen for the second time, what would you predict?
q3_a: The immune response would be slower because antibodies degrade over time
q3_b: The body would have no memory of the pathogen and react identically
q3_c: The immune response would be faster due to memory B cells

topic: How does diffusion work?
hook: Drop a drop of dye into still water and walk away — when you return, the colour will have spread on its own. How?
think_question: If diffusion didn't exist, how would oxygen reach every cell deep inside your body?
q1_text: What correctly describes diffusion?
q1_a: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high concentration toward low concentration
q1_b: Diffusion is the movement of water molecules only through a semipermeable membrane
q1_c: Diffusion is the process by which particles clump together under gravitational attraction
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of diffusion more useful than memorising the definition?
q2_a: Definitions are hard to remember, while mechanisms can be guessed from context
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Mechanisms are tested less frequently in school examinations than definitions
q3_text: If temperature were increased, what would you predict about the rate of diffusion?
q3_a: Diffusion would slow down because higher temperature makes particles too energetic to spread
q3_b: Diffusion would stop because particles become too heavy at high temperatures
q3_c: Diffusion would speed up because higher temperature increases particle kinetic energy

topic: Acids and bases inside everyday life
hook: Your blood must stay within a razor-thin pH range to keep you alive — just 0.4 outside normal can be fatal.
think_question: If you could neutralise ocean acidification by adjusting ocean pH, what unintended consequences might follow?
q1_text: What property defines an acid according to its behaviour in water?
q1_a: An acid releases hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water
q1_b: An acid releases hydroxide ions (OH-) when dissolved in water
q1_c: An acid absorbs all surrounding moisture and turns blue litmus red
q2_text: Why is understanding the acid-base mechanism more useful than just knowing pH numbers?
q2_a: Because pH numbers are not measurable in everyday kitchen experiments
q2_b: The mechanism explains why neutralisation occurs and lets you predict reactions
q2_c: Because the mechanism requires no mathematics and is simpler to use
q3_text: What would happen if you added more acid to a neutral salt solution?
q3_a: The solution would remain neutral because salt buffers all added acids
q3_b: The solution would turn basic because acid converts salts to bases
q3_c: The pH would drop below 7 and the solution would become acidic again

topic: Vectors: the mathematics of direction
hook: Two forces pulling you in opposite directions can cancel perfectly to zero. That maths is what holds bridges up.
think_question: Pilots use vector addition to fly straight despite crosswinds. What other professions silently depend on vector thinking?
q1_text: How does a vector quantity differ from a scalar quantity?
q1_a: A vector has both magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only
q1_b: A vector is always larger in value than its equivalent scalar
q1_c: A scalar requires two numbers to specify; a vector requires only one
q2_text: Why is using vector addition more useful than simple arithmetic addition for forces?
q2_a: Vector addition gives a larger resultant because it accounts for angles
q2_b: Vector addition reveals the actual net effect by accounting for both magnitude and direction
q2_c: Vector addition eliminates the need for trigonometry in physics problems
q3_text: If two equal forces are applied to an object at 180 degrees to each other, what is the net force?
q3_a: The net force equals the sum of the two magnitudes, acting in one direction
q3_b: The net force equals twice the magnitude of either force
q3_c: The net force is zero because the vectors cancel each other

topic: Electric potential and energy
hook: Lightning strikes from the sky — but the real energy story starts invisibly, long before the flash appears.
think_question: If you could harness all the electric potential energy in a single thunderstorm, how much of a city could it power?
q1_text: What does electric potential at a point in space represent?
q1_a: Work done per unit charge to bring a positive charge from infinity to that point
q1_b: The total charge accumulated on a conductor at that location
q1_c: The magnetic flux linking a current loop near that point
q2_text: Why does understanding potential as a mechanism help more than memorising its formula?
q2_a: The formula V = kQ/r is too complex for Class 12 students to apply
q2_b: Mechanism understanding lets you predict energy changes when charge moves
q2_c: Memorising the formula automatically gives the correct sign of potential
q3_text: If the distance from a positive charge doubles, what happens to electric potential there?
q3_a: It doubles because potential and distance are directly proportional
q3_b: It stays constant because potential depends only on the source charge
q3_c: It halves because electric potential is inversely proportional to distance

topic: How does blood know where to go?
hook: Your heart pumps 5 litres every minute through 100,000 km of vessels. What guides every single drop?
think_question: If surgeons could re-route blood vessels like roads on a map, which medical conditions could they cure?
q1_text: What guides blood to the correct organs in the circulatory system?
q1_a: Blood is pumped by the heart through a network of arteries, veins, and capillaries that form closed pathways to each organ.
q1_b: Blood cells have small magnets that attract them to specific organs needing oxygen.
q1_c: The brain sends electrical signals directly to red blood cells to direct their movement.
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of blood circulation more useful than simply knowing blood travels around the body?
q2_a: Blood circulation is the same in all animals, so the mechanism never changes.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: The heart pumps randomly, so there is no predictable mechanism to study.
q3_text: If a major artery supplying a muscle were blocked, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The muscle would receive more blood from veins to compensate for the blocked artery.
q3_b: The heart would beat slower to reduce pressure in the blocked vessel.
q3_c: The muscle would be deprived of oxygen and begin to fail or cramp.

topic: Why does your heart beat continuously?
hook: Your heart has beaten over 3 billion times by age 80 — without ever taking a break. What keeps it going?
think_question: Artificial pacemakers use electricity to regulate the heartbeat. What other organs might electrical implants eventually control?
q1_text: What keeps the heart beating without conscious effort?
q1_a: The sinoatrial node generates electrical impulses that trigger contractions
q1_b: Muscles in the chest wall compress the heart rhythmically
q1_c: Blood pressure forces the heart valves to open and close repeatedly
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of the heartbeat more useful than just knowing it beats?
q2_a: The heartbeat mechanism helps athletes run faster during exercise
q2_b: Knowing the mechanism allows us to understand heart disease and treatments
q2_c: Memorising the heartbeat rate is sufficient for all medical purposes
q3_text: If the sinoatrial node were damaged, what would you predict?
q3_a: The heart would beat faster to compensate for reduced signal strength
q3_b: Blood would circulate in the opposite direction through the veins
q3_c: The heart's rhythm would become irregular or stop

topic: Why does temperature change particle motion?
hook: Temperature is not what you feel — it's a measure of how violently invisible particles are bouncing inside matter.
think_question: If we could heat just the particles of one substance without heating the surrounding air, what technology might that enable?
q1_text: What is the relationship between temperature and the kinetic energy of particles?
q1_a: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance
q1_b: Temperature measures the total potential energy stored in chemical bonds between particles
q1_c: Temperature measures the number of particles present in a given volume of substance
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism linking temperature and particle motion important?
q2_a: It allows students to skip calculations and focus on written descriptions only
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: It is required only for physics and not for chemistry or biology topics
q3_text: If a gas were cooled significantly, what change in particle motion would you predict?
q3_a: The particles would gain energy and collide more forcefully with container walls
q3_b: The particles would reorganise into a new element with different chemical properties
q3_c: The particles would slow down and may eventually condense into a liquid or solid

topic: Why does antacid work?
hook: Your stomach acid is corrosive enough to burn skin — yet a tiny chalk tablet calms it in minutes. What happens?
think_question: If you could engineer an antacid that worked only in the stomach and nowhere else, how would that change medicine?
q1_text: How does antacid relieve acidity in the stomach?
q1_a: Antacid neutralises excess stomach acid through an acid-base reaction
q1_b: Antacid absorbs all food in the stomach to prevent acid production
q1_c: Antacid lowers body temperature so stomach cells stop producing acid
q2_text: Why is knowing the neutralisation mechanism more useful than just knowing antacids help?
q2_a: Because all antacids have identical chemical formulas and work identically
q2_b: The mechanism explains which bases work and predicts how much to take
q2_c: Because the mechanism is printed on packaging and removes guesswork
q3_text: What would happen if too much antacid were taken?
q3_a: The stomach pH would remain at 2 because the body regulates acidity strictly
q3_b: More acid would be produced to compensate for the neutralised acid
q3_c: The stomach would become too alkaline, causing discomfort and digestive problems

topic: What does velocity really mean?
hook: A car drives 60 km east then 60 km back — its average speed is 60 km/h, but its average velocity is zero. How?
think_question: In sport, does speed or velocity matter more — for a sprinter versus a long jumper? Does direction ever change the outcome?
q1_text: What distinguishes velocity from speed?
q1_a: Velocity is a vector quantity specifying both magnitude and direction of motion
q1_b: Velocity is always numerically greater than speed for the same motion
q1_c: Speed specifies direction while velocity gives only the rate of distance covered
q2_text: Why is knowing an object's velocity more useful than knowing only its speed?
q2_a: Velocity is always measured in SI units, making it more reliable
q2_b: Velocity reveals direction of motion, enabling prediction of future position
q2_c: Velocity removes the need to measure time intervals during motion
q3_text: A car travels 60 km east then 60 km west. What is its average velocity for the whole journey?
q3_a: 60 km/h east, because only the forward displacement counts
q3_b: 120 km divided by total time, giving a large positive value
q3_c: Zero, because the total displacement is zero

topic: Why capacitors store energy
hook: A camera flash charges for seconds, then releases all its energy in a single microsecond. What's doing the storing?
think_question: If capacitors could store as much energy as batteries but discharge in microseconds, how might that change electric vehicles?
q1_text: How does a capacitor store energy?
q1_a: By accumulating opposite charges on two separated conducting plates
q1_b: By converting electrical energy into chemical energy in a dielectric
q1_c: By producing a magnetic field between its two terminals
q2_text: Why is knowing the charge-separation mechanism in a capacitor useful?
q2_a: It makes it easier to remember the formula C = Q/V without derivation
q2_b: It explains why capacitance changes when a dielectric is inserted
q2_c: It proves that capacitors and batteries are interchangeable in circuits
q3_text: If a dielectric material is inserted between the plates of a charged capacitor, what changes?
q3_a: The charge on the plates increases because the dielectric adds free electrons
q3_b: The voltage across the plates increases to maintain the same stored charge
q3_c: The capacitance increases because the dielectric reduces the effective electric field

topic: Why do plants need sunlight?
hook: Plants eat light. They take invisible radiation from 150 million km away and turn it into sugar. How?
think_question: If we could install photosynthesis in human skin cells, how would that change our relationship with food?
q1_text: What is the main reason plants need sunlight?
q1_a: Sunlight provides energy for photosynthesis, the process by which plants make food from carbon dioxide and water.
q1_b: Sunlight heats the roots, which allows water to be absorbed more efficiently from the soil.
q1_c: Plants use sunlight to produce oxygen directly from the soil without needing carbon dioxide.
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of photosynthesis more useful than knowing that plants need sunlight?
q2_a: Plants grow identically in all light conditions, so the mechanism does not matter.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Only botanists need to understand photosynthesis; other students can memorise the fact.
q3_text: If a plant were kept in complete darkness for several weeks, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The plant would switch to absorbing nitrogen from the air to replace lost glucose.
q3_b: The plant would grow faster because darkness accelerates cell division in stems.
q3_c: The plant would be unable to make food, weaken, and eventually die.

topic: How do neurons carry information?
hook: A thought travels from your brain to your fingertip at 270 km/h — faster than a Formula 1 car. What's moving?
think_question: If scientists could record every neuron signal in a living brain in real time, what ethical questions would that raise?
q1_text: How do neurons transmit signals along their length?
q1_a: An electrical impulse called an action potential travels along the axon
q1_b: Neurons pass solid chemical pellets along hollow tubes to the brain
q1_c: Light signals travel through transparent neuron fibres to receptors
q2_text: Why is understanding the neural mechanism more useful than memorising nerve names?
q2_a: Nerve names are sufficient for understanding all neurological conditions
q2_b: It enables predictions about what happens when nerves are damaged
q2_c: Mechanisms only matter for motor neurons, not sensory neurons
q3_text: If the myelin sheath around a neuron were damaged, what would you predict?
q3_a: The neuron would generate stronger signals to overcome the damage
q3_b: The neuron would switch to chemical transmission instead of electrical
q3_c: Signal transmission would slow down or fail, causing nerve disorders

topic: Atoms: the tiny building blocks of everything
hook: If an atom were the size of a football stadium, its nucleus would be a marble at the centre. The rest is empty space.
think_question: If atoms are mostly empty space, why does matter feel solid? What would physics look like if atoms had no emptiness?
q1_text: Which statement best describes an atom?
q1_a: An atom is the smallest unit of an element retaining that element's chemical properties
q1_b: An atom is a cluster of molecules held together by surface tension forces
q1_c: An atom is a unit of energy that cannot be divided by any known process
q2_text: Why is understanding how atoms behave more useful than just memorising their definition?
q2_a: Definitions are optional knowledge, while behaviour is tested in every examination
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Atomic behaviour is simpler to learn because it involves only three rules
q3_text: If the number of protons in an atom were changed, what would you predict?
q3_a: The mass of the atom would stay identical because protons have negligible mass
q3_b: The atom's electron shells would collapse because electrons depend on neutrons
q3_c: The atom would become a different element with different chemical properties

topic: Metals: why are they useful?
hook: The electrons in a metal are so loosely attached they wander freely — which is exactly why metal lights up your room.
think_question: If we discovered a metal that was stronger than steel and lighter than aluminium at room temperature, what would it replace?
q1_text: Which property of metals makes them useful for electrical wiring?
q1_a: Metals have free electrons that allow easy conduction of electricity
q1_b: Metals have tightly bound electrons that block electrical current flow
q1_c: Metals conduct electricity because they are transparent to photons
q2_text: Why is understanding the metallic bonding mechanism more useful than listing metal uses?
q2_a: Because listing uses requires memorisation while mechanism requires no memory
q2_b: The mechanism explains conductivity, malleability and ductility all at once
q2_c: Because metallic bonding is the same in all materials including plastics
q3_text: What would happen to a metal's conductivity if its free electrons were removed?
q3_a: Conductivity would increase because fewer electrons create less resistance
q3_b: The metal would conduct only heat but not electricity without free electrons
q3_c: The metal would lose conductivity and behave more like an insulator

topic: Why objects accelerate
hook: Drop a feather and a bowling ball on the Moon — they hit the ground at exactly the same time. Newton explains why.
think_question: If you could double Earth's gravitational field overnight, which human technologies would immediately stop working?
q1_text: What causes an object to accelerate according to Newton's second law?
q1_a: A net unbalanced force acting on the object
q1_b: The object's inherent tendency to speed up over time
q1_c: An increase in the object's mass during motion
q2_text: Why is understanding the net force more useful than knowing an object's instantaneous speed?
q2_a: Net force tells us the mass of the object without measuring it
q2_b: Net force reveals the cause-and-effect mechanism that predicts how motion will change
q2_c: Net force is constant for all objects regardless of mass
q3_text: If the net force on an object is doubled while its mass stays the same, what happens to acceleration?
q3_a: Acceleration halves because force and acceleration are inversely proportional
q3_b: Acceleration remains unchanged since mass has not changed
q3_c: Acceleration doubles, since a = F/m and F has doubled

topic: How circuits really behave
hook: Every USB charger, solar panel, and power grid is governed by two laws Kirchhoff wrote in 1845. Still undefeated.
think_question: If Kirchhoff's laws broke down at very high currents, how would that limit the future of electrical engineering?
q1_text: What do Kirchhoff's laws describe about circuit behaviour?
q1_a: Conservation of charge at junctions and conservation of energy around loops
q1_b: The relationship between magnetic flux and induced current in a loop
q1_c: How resistance changes with temperature in metallic conductors
q2_text: Why is understanding circuit mechanisms better than memorising Ohm's law alone?
q2_a: Ohm's law is only valid for AC circuits, not for DC circuits
q2_b: Mechanism understanding lets you analyse complex multi-loop circuits correctly
q2_c: Memorising Ohm's law is sufficient for all Class 12 circuit problems
q3_text: If you add a resistor in parallel to an existing resistor in a circuit, what happens to total resistance?
q3_a: Total resistance increases because more components are added to the circuit
q3_b: Total resistance remains unchanged because parallel paths do not interact
q3_c: Total resistance decreases because additional current paths reduce overall opposition

topic: How does a seed know which way to grow?
hook: Plant a seed upside down in total darkness — the root still grows down and the shoot still grows up. How does it know?
think_question: If you could override a plant's gravitational sense, could you grow plants in any direction you wanted in space?
q1_text: What is the main mechanism that tells a seed's root to grow downward and shoot to grow upward?
q1_a: A process called gravitropism makes roots grow toward gravity and shoots grow away from it.
q1_b: Seeds detect the colour of soil and grow their roots toward darker regions.
q1_c: The seed's outer coat has markings that orient the embryo correctly before germination.
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of directional growth more useful than just observing that roots grow down?
q2_a: Roots always grow in random directions, so there is no mechanism to study.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Seed growth direction is determined only by the farmer planting the seed correctly.
q3_text: If a germinating seed were grown in a rotating drum that cancelled out the effect of gravity, what would you predict?
q3_a: The root would grow faster because less gravity means less resistance to elongation.
q3_b: The shoot would grow downward because photosynthesis requires the leaves to face the soil.
q3_c: The root and shoot would grow in random directions, unable to use gravity as a guide.

topic: Why do we have fingerprints?
hook: Your fingerprints are unique to you — but so are those of your identical twin. What's going on at the microscopic level?
think_question: If fingerprints could regrow differently after injury, would forensic identification still work?
q1_text: What is the primary function of fingerprint ridges on human skin?
q1_a: Fingerprint ridges improve grip by increasing friction between skin and objects
q1_b: Fingerprints regulate sweat distribution to keep palms dry
q1_c: Fingerprint patterns identify nerves under the skin for better sensation
q2_text: Why is understanding why fingerprints exist more useful than just describing their patterns?
q2_a: Pattern descriptions are sufficient for forensic science applications
q2_b: Understanding function allows predictions about people who lack fingerprints
q2_c: Fingerprint function only matters for primates, not humans specifically
q3_text: If fingerprint ridges were completely smooth, what would you predict?
q3_a: People would develop stronger nails to compensate for grip loss
q3_b: Sweat glands in the fingertip would become more active instead
q3_c: Grip on smooth or wet surfaces would be significantly reduced

topic: How was the atom discovered?
hook: Scientists once thought atoms were solid spheres. One experiment shattered that idea — most particles went straight through.
think_question: If Rutherford's gold foil experiment had shown no deflection at all, what atomic model would we teach today?
q1_text: Which experiment provided the first evidence that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus?
q1_a: Rutherford's gold foil experiment, where alpha particles were deflected at large angles
q1_b: Dalton's law experiment, where gases combined in fixed volume ratios at constant pressure
q1_c: Thomson's cathode ray experiment, which showed that electrons orbit the nucleus in shells
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of the gold foil experiment more valuable than memorising its result?
q2_a: Results change every year but mechanisms stay constant and are never re-examined
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: The mechanism involves maths which is more reliable than descriptive results
q3_text: If all alpha particles had passed straight through the gold foil without deflection, what would that predict?
q3_a: The nucleus would be confirmed to be large and spread throughout the atom
q3_b: The experiment would show that electrons repel alpha particles near the surface
q3_c: The atom would likely have no dense nucleus, contradicting the nuclear model

topic: Why does corrosion happen?
hook: Iron rusts red, copper turns green, silver goes black — every metal decays differently, and each tells a chemical story.
think_question: Some Roman iron tools survived 2,000 years without rusting. What secret of theirs could modern engineering borrow?
q1_text: What causes iron to corrode (rust) when exposed to air and moisture?
q1_a: Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide (rust)
q1_b: Iron reacts with nitrogen in air to form a brittle iron nitride layer
q1_c: Iron loses carbon atoms to the atmosphere, weakening its structure
q2_text: Why is understanding the oxidation mechanism of corrosion more useful than noting it happens?
q2_a: Because all metals corrode identically so the mechanism is universal
q2_b: Knowing the mechanism explains which conditions accelerate or prevent corrosion
q2_c: Because the mechanism proves corrosion is beneficial and should not be stopped
q3_text: What would happen to iron corrosion if oxygen were completely removed from the environment?
q3_a: Corrosion would accelerate because iron reacts faster without oxygen competition
q3_b: The rate of rusting would stay the same as moisture is the only factor
q3_c: Corrosion would stop or greatly slow because oxygen is essential for rusting

topic: Newton's laws in the real world
hook: Every rocket launch, car crash, and sporting tackle follows the same three rules Newton discovered 350 years ago.
think_question: If friction suddenly disappeared from Earth's surface, name three technologies that would immediately stop working.
q1_text: Which of Newton's laws explains why a passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly?
q1_a: Newton's first law: the passenger's body continues moving forward due to inertia
q1_b: Newton's third law: the bus pushes the passenger in the direction of motion
q1_c: Newton's second law: braking creates a backward force that multiplies passenger mass
q2_text: Why is Newton's third law more useful than just knowing a force's magnitude?
q2_a: Newton's third law removes the need to measure friction in real systems
q2_b: It reveals that every interaction involves paired equal-and-opposite forces, enabling prediction
q2_c: It shows that action forces are always greater than reaction forces in practice
q3_text: If a rocket expels exhaust gases at a higher speed, how does that affect the rocket's thrust?
q3_a: Thrust decreases because faster exhaust reduces mass flow rate
q3_b: Thrust stays the same since the rocket mass has not changed
q3_c: Thrust increases because greater exhaust momentum produces a larger reaction force

topic: Why AC electricity is used in power grids
hook: The War of Currents between Edison and Tesla shaped every power socket on Earth. Why did AC ultimately win?
think_question: Now that DC can be converted efficiently, should we replace AC power grids? What would we gain and what would we lose?
q1_text: Why is alternating current preferred for long-distance power transmission?
q1_a: AC voltage can be stepped up by transformers, reducing transmission-line losses
q1_b: AC electrons travel faster than DC electrons through copper wires
q1_c: AC current never experiences resistance unlike DC current in cables
q2_text: Why is understanding the transformer mechanism important for AC grids?
q2_a: It proves that DC power lines are physically impossible to construct
q2_b: It explains how voltage is raised and lowered efficiently across the grid
q2_c: It shows that AC frequency must always equal 50 Hz worldwide
q3_text: If the transmission voltage is doubled, what happens to power lost as heat in the cables?
q3_a: Power loss doubles because higher voltage forces more current through the cable
q3_b: Power loss stays the same because resistance of cables does not change with voltage
q3_c: Power loss falls to one-quarter because loss is proportional to current squared

topic: Why do some materials float while others sink?
hook: A massive steel ship floats, but a tiny steel coin sinks. The difference isn't weight — it's something far more clever.
think_question: Deep-sea fish are crushed if brought to the surface too fast. What does that tell us about pressure and density in the ocean?
q1_text: What determines whether an object floats or sinks in water?
q1_a: An object floats if its density is less than water and sinks if its density is greater than water.
q1_b: An object floats if it is made of natural materials and sinks if it is made of synthetic ones.
q1_c: An object floats only if it is hollow and sinks only if it is completely solid.
q2_text: Why is understanding density and buoyancy more useful than just knowing which objects float?
q2_a: Every object floats in water, so there is no need to understand the mechanism.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Buoyancy only applies to water, so the mechanism has no real-world applications.
q3_text: If you added salt to water until it became very dense, what would you predict would happen to an egg placed in it?
q3_a: The egg would sink faster because salt increases the gravitational pull on objects.
q3_b: The egg would dissolve because salt reacts chemically with the eggshell.
q3_c: The egg would float because the saltwater's density becomes greater than the egg's density.

topic: The science of friction
hook: Without friction, you couldn't walk, write, or pick up a cup. The invisible grip between surfaces shapes your whole day.
think_question: If engineers designed a material with exactly the right friction — not too much, not too little — where would it help most?
q1_text: What causes friction between two surfaces?
q1_a: Microscopic irregularities on surfaces interlock and resist sliding motion
q1_b: Friction is caused by static electricity attracting surfaces together
q1_c: Air molecules trapped between surfaces push back against movement
q2_text: Why is knowing how friction works more useful than just knowing it slows things down?
q2_a: Knowing friction slows things down is enough for all engineering problems
q2_b: Understanding friction helps engineers design brakes, tyres, and lubricants
q2_c: Friction mechanisms are only relevant to physics, not everyday engineering
q3_text: If a lubricant were applied between two sliding surfaces, what would you predict?
q3_a: Friction would increase because the lubricant adds extra mass to surfaces
q3_b: Surfaces would bond together as the lubricant hardens under pressure
q3_c: Friction would decrease because the lubricant separates the surfaces

topic: Why are some atoms radioactive?
hook: Some atoms are quietly falling apart right now — releasing invisible energy that can penetrate solid walls.
think_question: Nuclear medicine uses radioactive atoms to detect cancer. If you could control which atoms were radioactive and when, what else could you treat?
q1_text: What causes an atom to be radioactive?
q1_a: An unstable nucleus spontaneously emits radiation to achieve a more stable nuclear configuration
q1_b: An atom becomes radioactive when it gains extra electrons from a nearby charged object
q1_c: Radioactivity occurs when atoms absorb too much sunlight and re-emit it as particles
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of radioactive decay more useful than just knowing it emits radiation?
q2_a: Knowing radiation exists is sufficient for safety; mechanisms are only for scientists
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: The mechanism helps calculate tax on nuclear materials in industrial settings
q3_text: If a radioactive isotope lost neutrons until its nucleus became stable, what would you predict?
q3_a: The atom would continue emitting stronger and stronger radiation indefinitely
q3_b: The atom would split into two equal halves and both halves would remain radioactive
q3_c: The rate of radioactive emission would decrease and eventually the atom would become stable

topic: How can corrosion be prevented?
hook: The Statue of Liberty was originally shiny copper and turned green within 20 years. Was that protection or decay?
think_question: If self-healing metals could repair corrosion damage automatically, which industries would benefit most?
q1_text: Which method prevents corrosion by coating iron with a sacrificial metal?
q1_a: Galvanisation coats iron with zinc, which corrodes preferentially instead
q1_b: Anodisation coats iron with copper to create a decorative barrier
q1_c: Electroplating coats iron with carbon to block all chemical reactions
q2_text: Why is understanding the protective mechanism more important than just listing prevention methods?
q2_a: Because prevention methods never work and understanding explains why
q2_b: The mechanism reveals why some coatings fail over time while others succeed
q2_c: Because all prevention methods use identical chemical principles anyway
q3_text: What would happen if a zinc coating on galvanised steel got scratched deeply?
q3_a: The iron would rust immediately because scratching removes all protection
q3_b: The iron would become more resistant because scratching hardens the surface
q3_c: Zinc would still corrode preferentially, protecting the exposed iron nearby

topic: Why astronauts feel weightless
hook: Astronauts aren't weightless because gravity is gone — gravity still pulls them hard. So why do they float?
think_question: If a spacecraft could create artificial gravity by spinning, what engineering challenges would that solve and create?
q1_text: Why do astronauts in orbit feel weightless despite gravity still acting on them?
q1_a: They are in free fall, so no normal contact force acts on them
q1_b: Gravity becomes zero at orbital altitude above Earth's surface
q1_c: The spacecraft generates an anti-gravity field that cancels Earth's pull
q2_text: Why is understanding free fall more useful than saying 'there is no gravity in space'?
q2_a: Free fall allows astronauts to produce gravity by spinning the spacecraft
q2_b: Free fall correctly identifies the mechanism: gravity acts but no surface reaction force exists
q2_c: Free fall proves that gravity diminishes to zero within 200 km of Earth
q3_text: If the orbital speed of a spacecraft were suddenly reduced, what would happen?
q3_a: The spacecraft would float outward into a higher orbit due to reduced centripetal force
q3_b: Gravity would still not affect the spacecraft since it is already in orbit
q3_c: The spacecraft would fall toward Earth as gravity is no longer balanced by orbital velocity

topic: Electromagnetism: electricity creating magnetism
hook: Run a current through a wire and a magnetic field appears from nothing. Switch off the current and it vanishes completely.
think_question: Electromagnets can be switched on and off, permanent magnets cannot. What future technologies might need switchable magnetism?
q1_text: What does a current-carrying conductor produce around itself?
q1_a: A magnetic field whose strength depends on the current and wire geometry
q1_b: An electric field that repels nearby positive charges uniformly
q1_c: A gravitational field proportional to the mass of moving electrons
q2_text: Why is the concept of magnetic field as a mechanism more useful than just knowing the right-hand rule?
q2_a: The right-hand rule is only applicable to solenoids, not straight wires
q2_b: Understanding the mechanism lets you predict field direction for any current shape
q2_c: Knowing the rule is sufficient; mechanisms are not tested in Class 12
q3_text: If the current through a solenoid is doubled, what happens to the magnetic field inside?
q3_a: The field halves because more current causes electrons to cancel each other
q3_b: The field remains constant because it depends only on the number of turns
q3_c: The field doubles because magnetic field in a solenoid is directly proportional to current

topic: The hidden world inside a drop of water
hook: A single drop of pond water can contain millions of living creatures — none of them visible to the naked eye.
think_question: If microorganisms could be engineered to clean polluted water, what trade-offs would you need to consider?
q1_text: What is found in a drop of pond water that cannot be seen with the naked eye?
q1_a: Microscopic living organisms such as bacteria, algae, and protozoa exist in a drop of pond water.
q1_b: A drop of water contains tiny air pockets that give it its round shape on surfaces.
q1_c: Water droplets contain dissolved minerals arranged in crystal patterns invisible to the eye.
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism of what makes water life-supporting more useful than just knowing microbes exist?
q2_a: All microbes are harmful, so understanding them has no benefit for students.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Microbes in water are destroyed by oxygen, so the mechanism is always the same.
q3_text: If the water in a pond were heated to a very high temperature, what would you predict would happen to the microorganisms?
q3_a: The microorganisms would grow larger because heat provides them with more energy.
q3_b: The microorganisms would move to the bottom of the pond to avoid the heat.
q3_c: Most microorganisms would be killed by the heat, drastically reducing their population.

topic: Why can a giant ship float?
hook: A steel aircraft carrier weighs 100,000 tonnes — yet floats serenely on water. The maths behind this is over 2,000 years old.
think_question: If you could reduce a ship's density without reducing its strength, what future materials might make that possible?
q1_text: What principle explains why a massive steel ship can float on water?
q1_a: Archimedes' principle: the ship displaces water equal to its weight
q1_b: Steel becomes less dense when heated by the sun on open oceans
q1_c: Air currents beneath the hull push the ship upward like a wing
q2_text: Why does understanding buoyancy as a mechanism matter more than memorising that ships float?
q2_a: Memorising that ships float is sufficient for all naval engineering
q2_b: It lets engineers predict how much cargo a ship can safely carry
q2_c: Buoyancy mechanisms only apply to wooden boats, not steel ones
q3_text: If a ship took on water and became denser than water overall, what would you predict?
q3_a: The ship would rise higher in the water due to increased internal pressure
q3_b: The ship's buoyancy force would increase to balance the extra weight
q3_c: The ship would sink because upthrust would no longer equal the total weight

topic: What makes an element different from another?
hook: Change one proton in a gold atom and it becomes mercury. Change one more and it becomes thallium. Proton number is destiny.
think_question: If scientists could routinely add or remove protons from atoms, would turning lead into gold ever become practically useful?
q1_text: What property uniquely identifies and distinguishes one element from all others?
q1_a: The number of protons in the nucleus, the atomic number, uniquely defines each element
q1_b: The colour and texture of the element in its solid form at room temperature
q1_c: The total mass of the element including all isotopes averaged across the periodic table
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism that makes elements different more valuable than listing their properties?
q2_a: Properties change with temperature, making them less reliable than any mechanism
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Listing properties is required for industrial applications while mechanisms are theoretical
q3_text: If two atoms had the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, what would you predict?
q3_a: They would be completely different elements with entirely different chemical behaviours
q3_b: They would be oppositely charged ions that attract each other strongly in solution
q3_c: They would be isotopes of the same element with slightly different masses but similar chemistry

topic: Carbon: the element behind life
hook: Carbon is the fourth most abundant element in the universe, yet it forms more compounds than all others combined.
think_question: Silicon is carbon's neighbour on the periodic table. If silicon-based life existed, where in the universe might it live?
q1_text: Why is carbon called the element behind life?
q1_a: Carbon forms four covalent bonds, enabling complex chains and ring structures
q1_b: Carbon is the heaviest element and sinks to the core of all living cells
q1_c: Carbon is the most abundant element in Earth's crust and atmosphere
q2_text: Why is understanding carbon's bonding mechanism more useful than memorising its uses?
q2_a: Because memorised uses of carbon apply only to diamond and graphite
q2_b: The bonding mechanism explains why carbon forms millions of different compounds
q2_c: Because carbon's uses change annually so only the mechanism stays relevant
q3_text: What would happen to life on Earth if carbon could only form two bonds instead of four?
q3_a: Life would be more complex because simpler atoms create more diverse molecules
q3_b: Life would remain the same because bond number does not affect molecule diversity
q3_c: Carbon could not form complex molecules, making most biological molecules impossible

topic: Conservation of momentum
hook: When billiard balls collide, something invisible transfers between them perfectly — and physicists predict the outcome before it happens.
think_question: Rocket engines work in vacuum because of momentum conservation. Could this principle power vehicles on Earth more efficiently?
q1_text: In an isolated system, what happens to total momentum when two objects collide?
q1_a: Total momentum is conserved; it remains constant before and after collision
q1_b: Total momentum increases because kinetic energy is transferred between objects
q1_c: Total momentum decreases due to the heat generated during impact
q2_text: Why is the conservation of momentum principle more useful than simply measuring impact forces?
q2_a: Momentum conservation eliminates the need to measure mass in any calculation
q2_b: It provides a cause-and-effect law that predicts outcomes without knowing collision details
q2_c: Impact forces are always greater than momentum changes, making forces irrelevant
q3_text: If a stationary ball of mass 2 kg is hit by a 1 kg ball moving at 4 m/s and they stick together, what is the final speed?
q3_a: 4 m/s, because the moving ball transfers all its speed to the system
q3_b: 2 m/s, because speed is shared equally between the two balls
q3_c: Approximately 1.33 m/s, from conservation of momentum (4 kg m/s / 3 kg)

topic: How electric motors work
hook: Your electric toothbrush, the car passing you on the road, the pump in your hospital — all run on an 1820 discovery.
think_question: If motors could recover 100% of energy during braking, how would that change the design of electric cars?
q1_text: What is the principle behind an electric motor converting electrical to mechanical energy?
q1_a: A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque that makes it rotate
q1_b: Resistance heating in the coil causes it to expand and drive a shaft
q1_c: Changing voltage in the coil creates pressure that pushes the rotor outward
q2_text: Why does understanding the force-on-current mechanism matter in motor design?
q2_a: It proves motors only work with DC and never with AC supply
q2_b: It allows engineers to predict torque and improve motor efficiency
q2_c: It shows that the commutator is unnecessary in all modern motors
q3_text: If the magnetic field strength inside a motor is doubled, what happens to the torque?
q3_a: Torque halves because a stronger field opposes the coil's rotation
q3_b: Torque remains unchanged because torque depends only on current, not field
q3_c: Torque doubles because the force on a current-carrying conductor is proportional to field strength

topic: Why does ice float on water?
hook: Ice floating on water is so rare in nature it may be the reason life exists on Earth. What would happen if it sank?
think_question: If water ice were denser than liquid water like most substances, how would life in Earth's oceans be different today?
q1_text: What is the main reason ice floats on liquid water?
q1_a: Ice is less dense than liquid water because water molecules form a hexagonal crystal structure when frozen, taking up more space.
q1_b: Ice floats because it contains trapped air bubbles that make it lighter than water.
q1_c: Ice floats because its surface is smoother, reducing the friction that would make it sink.
q2_text: Why is understanding the molecular structure of ice more useful than knowing that ice floats?
q2_a: Ice always sinks in warm water, so the molecular explanation is incorrect.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: The floating of ice is only important in polar regions and not relevant elsewhere.
q3_text: What would happen to aquatic life in lakes if ice were denser than water and sank to the bottom?
q3_a: Fish would swim to the surface in winter because warm water rises to replace sinking ice.
q3_b: Lakes would freeze more slowly because sunlight would not be blocked by a floating ice layer.
q3_c: Lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up, killing most aquatic life in winter.

topic: How does pressure change with depth?
hook: At the deepest ocean trench, the pressure equals 50 jumbo jets stacked on top of you — and life still exists there.
think_question: If humans could survive extreme deep-sea pressure without equipment, what ocean resources could we access that are now impossible?
q1_text: What happens to water pressure as you go deeper underwater?
q1_a: Pressure increases with depth because the weight of water above increases
q1_b: Pressure decreases with depth because there is less air below the surface
q1_c: Pressure stays constant at any depth because water is incompressible
q2_text: Why is understanding the pressure-depth mechanism useful?
q2_a: Memorising that deep water is dangerous is sufficient for all purposes
q2_b: It helps predict safe diving depths and design submarines and pipelines
q2_c: Pressure mechanisms only matter for gases, not liquids like water
q3_text: If a submarine descended to twice the depth, what would you predict about external pressure?
q3_a: External pressure would remain the same because water density is constant
q3_b: Pressure would decrease as colder water is less able to exert force
q3_c: External pressure would approximately double due to greater water weight above

topic: How do chemical bonds hold matter together?
hook: The bond between two atoms is invisible and smaller than any instrument can touch — yet it holds together every solid thing you see.
think_question: If we could design custom chemical bonds on demand, what material properties would you engineer that don't exist in nature?
q1_text: What is the correct description of how ionic bonds form?
q1_a: Ionic bonds form when one atom transfers electrons to another, creating attracting oppositely charged ions
q1_b: Ionic bonds form when two atoms share electrons equally in overlapping outer orbitals
q1_c: Ionic bonds form when atoms merge their nuclei together under high temperature and pressure
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of chemical bonding more useful than memorising bond definitions?
q2_a: Bond definitions are too long to memorise, so mechanisms replace them in advanced study
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Mechanisms are shorter and therefore easier to write in limited examination time
q3_text: If an atom with one outer electron bonded with an atom that needed one electron, what would form?
q3_a: A covalent compound where both atoms share their electrons equally across all shells
q3_b: A metallic lattice because single-electron atoms always form metallic structures
q3_c: An ionic compound where the electron transfers, forming a positive and negative ion pair

topic: Why can carbon form millions of compounds?
hook: Carbon atoms can chain, branch, and ring together in endless combinations — which is why life as we know it exists.
think_question: Chemists have synthesised millions of carbon compounds that don't occur in nature. Could one replace plastic without the environmental damage?
q1_text: What unique property of carbon allows it to form millions of compounds?
q1_a: Carbon can bond with itself and other atoms in chains, branches and rings
q1_b: Carbon has the highest atomic mass among non-metals, allowing many reactions
q1_c: Carbon exists in liquid form at room temperature, enabling flexible bonding
q2_text: Why does understanding carbon's catenation mechanism matter more than listing compounds?
q2_a: Because listing compounds is impossible since there are millions of them
q2_b: The catenation mechanism explains why carbon chemistry underlies all organic life
q2_c: Because catenation only applies to carbon and cannot explain anything else
q3_text: What would happen to the variety of organic compounds if carbon could not bond to itself?
q3_a: The variety would increase because carbon would form stronger bonds with other atoms
q3_b: The number of compounds would stay the same since other atoms form chains too
q3_c: Organic chemistry would be extremely limited with very few carbon compounds possible

topic: How rockets work
hook: Rockets accelerate by throwing mass backwards — there's nothing to push against in space, so Newton's third law does all the work.
think_question: If humanity needed to leave Earth in under 50 years, what rocket technology advances would be most critical?
q1_text: Which physical principle explains how a rocket accelerates in the vacuum of space?
q1_a: Newton's third law: exhaust gases pushed backward propel the rocket forward
q1_b: Bernoulli's principle: faster gas flow below the rocket creates upward lift
q1_c: Archimedes' principle: the rocket displaces air to generate buoyant thrust
q2_text: Why is understanding rocket propulsion through Newton's third law more useful than knowing fuel burn rate?
q2_a: Newton's third law shows that rockets can operate without fuel in deep space
q2_b: It reveals the cause-and-effect mechanism linking exhaust momentum to rocket acceleration
q2_c: Fuel burn rate is irrelevant since thrust depends only on exhaust temperature
q3_text: If a rocket expels the same exhaust mass but at twice the velocity, how does thrust change?
q3_a: Thrust halves because the exhaust takes longer to leave the engine
q3_b: Thrust is unchanged since mass flow rate is the same
q3_c: Thrust doubles because momentum of exhaust is proportional to its velocity

topic: How generators work
hook: Almost all electricity on Earth — wind, coal, nuclear, hydro — comes from the same trick: spinning a magnet near a coil.
think_question: If a generator could be made small enough to wear, what human motion could power your devices throughout the day?
q1_text: What is the core principle by which a generator produces electricity?
q1_a: A rotating coil in a magnetic field experiences changing flux, inducing an EMF
q1_b: Chemical reactions in the coil convert heat directly into electrical current
q1_c: Friction between the rotor and stator strips electrons from the conductor
q2_text: Why is Faraday's law of induction the key mechanism for generators?
q2_a: It states that voltage equals current divided by time, simplifying generator design
q2_b: It quantifies how changing magnetic flux through a coil produces EMF
q2_c: It proves that AC generators always produce exactly 220 V output
q3_text: If a generator's coil spins twice as fast, what happens to the induced EMF?
q3_a: EMF halves because faster rotation reduces the time flux is changing
q3_b: EMF stays the same because the magnetic field inside the generator is fixed
q3_c: EMF doubles because the rate of change of magnetic flux increases with speed

topic: How does a refrigerator actually cool things?
hook: A fridge doesn't create coldness — it moves heat somewhere else. There's no such thing as 'cold energy'. What's happening?
think_question: If fridge-style heat pumps replaced all gas boilers in homes, how much carbon could be removed from domestic energy use?
q1_text: What is the basic mechanism by which a refrigerator cools food?
q1_a: A refrigerant fluid circulates through coils, evaporating inside the fridge to absorb heat and condensing outside to release it.
q1_b: The refrigerator generates cold air by spinning a fan through ice water stored in the back panel.
q1_c: Electric current flowing through metal coils directly absorbs heat from the food inside.
q2_text: Why is understanding the refrigeration cycle more useful than knowing that a refrigerator keeps things cold?
q2_a: Refrigerators produce cold from nothing, so there is no mechanism to explain.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: All appliances work the same way, so understanding one mechanism explains nothing new.
q3_text: If the refrigerant fluid in a refrigerator leaked out completely, what would you predict would happen?
q3_a: The fridge would cool more efficiently because air conducts cold better than refrigerant.
q3_b: The compressor would produce more electrical energy to compensate for the missing refrigerant.
q3_c: The refrigerator would stop cooling because there is no fluid to carry heat away from inside.

topic: Why does a balloon expand at high altitude?
hook: Weather balloons swell to the size of a house before popping — just from air pressure dropping as they rise.
think_question: If you inhaled from a balloon at high altitude then came back to sea level, what would happen to your lungs and why?
q1_text: Why does a sealed balloon get bigger when it rises to high altitude?
q1_a: Atmospheric pressure decreases at altitude, allowing the gas inside to expand
q1_b: Warmer temperatures at altitude cause the rubber to stretch outward
q1_c: Gravity decreases at altitude so gas molecules spread apart naturally
q2_text: Why is knowing the mechanism of gas expansion more useful than just observing it expands?
q2_a: Observing the expansion is enough to design weather balloons accurately
q2_b: It enables predictions about balloon volume at different altitudes or pressures
q2_c: Gas expansion mechanisms only apply to helium, not to air-filled balloons
q3_text: If a balloon were taken deep underwater instead, what would you predict?
q3_a: The balloon would expand as water is denser and pushes gas outward
q3_b: The balloon would stay the same size as water pressure is uniform
q3_c: The balloon would shrink because increased pressure compresses the gas inside

topic: Why does mass stay conserved in a reaction?
hook: Burn a log until nothing remains but ash — weigh everything including the smoke, and nothing has disappeared.
think_question: If a future reaction truly violated conservation of mass by even a tiny amount, what would that mean for all of physics?
q1_text: What does the law of conservation of mass state about a chemical reaction?
q1_a: Total reactant mass equals total product mass; atoms are neither created nor destroyed
q1_b: Mass increases in every reaction because energy is converted into additional matter
q1_c: Mass is conserved only in physical changes but always changes in chemical reactions
q2_text: Why is understanding the atomic mechanism of mass conservation more useful than just stating the law?
q2_a: The law is outdated, so the mechanism provides a more modern and accurate description
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Memorising the law is sufficient for all practical laboratory and industrial purposes
q3_text: If a metal burned completely in air and the ash seemed lighter, what prediction explains this correctly?
q3_a: Some atoms were destroyed in the intense heat of the combustion reaction
q3_b: The metal released protons that escaped into the atmosphere, reducing its mass
q3_c: Some product gases escaped into the air; total mass including gases is still conserved

topic: How soap actually removes dirt
hook: Soap is a molecular key — one end grabs oil, the other grabs water, forcing the two to coexist and carry dirt away.
think_question: If you could engineer a soap-like molecule with no environmental toxicity that cleaned better than detergents, where would you start?
q1_text: How does soap remove oil-based dirt from skin?
q1_a: Soap molecules have a water-loving head and oil-loving tail that trap dirt
q1_b: Soap dissolves all oils by converting them into water-soluble acids
q1_c: Soap neutralises all dirt chemically, breaking it down into harmless gases
q2_text: Why is understanding the micelle mechanism of soap more useful than knowing it cleans?
q2_a: Because micelles are visible to the naked eye and easy to demonstrate
q2_b: The mechanism explains why soap works on oil but water alone cannot remove it
q2_c: Because the mechanism proves that any liquid can replace soap for cleaning
q3_text: What would happen to soap's cleaning ability in hard water with high mineral content?
q3_a: Soap would clean more efficiently because minerals help break down grease
q3_b: Soap would clean identically because water hardness does not affect micelles
q3_c: Soap would lose effectiveness because minerals react with it to form scum

topic: Rotational motion: why wheels matter
hook: A wheel rolls without slipping — yet the bottom of the wheel, at every instant, is actually completely still. How?
think_question: Flywheels store enormous energy by spinning. Could city buses run entirely on flywheel energy between stops?
q1_text: What is the rotational equivalent of linear inertia called?
q1_a: Moment of inertia, which depends on mass distribution about the rotation axis
q1_b: Angular velocity, which measures how fast the object completes each rotation
q1_c: Torque, which is the rotational form of linear momentum
q2_text: Why is understanding torque more useful than knowing only a wheel's rotational speed?
q2_a: Torque indicates the colour of the rotational field around the wheel
q2_b: Torque explains the cause of rotation, enabling prediction of angular acceleration
q2_c: Torque replaces the need to measure angular displacement in wheel design
q3_text: If the radius at which a force is applied to a wheel is doubled, what happens to the torque produced?
q3_a: Torque halves because the moment arm becomes less efficient at greater distances
q3_b: Torque stays the same since only the applied force determines rotation
q3_c: Torque doubles because torque = force multiplied by perpendicular distance

topic: Maxwell's great unification
hook: In 1865, Maxwell predicted radio waves from pure mathematics — 23 years before anyone built a radio. How confident was he?
think_question: Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism. If a future physicist unified gravity with the other forces, what technology might follow?
q1_text: What did Maxwell's equations unify into a single framework?
q1_a: Electricity and magnetism as two aspects of one electromagnetic interaction
q1_b: Gravity and nuclear forces into a single field equation
q1_c: Thermodynamics and electrostatics into a combined energy principle
q2_text: Why was Maxwell's prediction of electromagnetic waves a landmark in physics?
q2_a: It replaced Newton's laws, making mechanics obsolete for all purposes
q2_b: It showed that changing fields can propagate through space without a medium
q2_c: It proved that light travels at different speeds in different reference frames
q3_text: If Maxwell had found that electromagnetic waves needed a medium to travel, what would follow?
q3_a: Radio signals would travel faster in vacuum than in glass fibres
q3_b: Television would work better in air than in underground cables
q3_c: Light could not travel through the vacuum of space to reach Earth from the Sun

topic: Why do shadows change during the day?
hook: Your shadow is longest in the morning, shortest at noon, and long again at evening. What invisible clock drives this?
think_question: Before clocks were invented, people used shadow length to tell time. Could shadow-based timekeeping ever be precise enough for science?
q1_text: What is the main reason shadows change length and direction during the day?
q1_a: As the Earth rotates, the Sun's apparent position in the sky changes, altering the angle of light and therefore the shadow's length and direction.
q1_b: The Moon's gravitational pull bends sunlight differently at different times of the day.
q1_c: Shadows change because the temperature of the air bends light rays by different amounts.
q2_text: Why is understanding Earth's rotation more useful than just observing that shadows move?
q2_a: Shadows are caused by clouds, so Earth's rotation plays no role in their movement.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Shadow movement is random and cannot be predicted by any mechanism.
q3_text: If you measured the length of your shadow at noon and again at 4 PM, what would you predict?
q3_a: The shadow would be longer at noon because the Sun is directly overhead and very hot.
q3_b: The shadow would be the same length because the Sun moves at a constant speed.
q3_c: The shadow would be longer at 4 PM because the Sun is lower in the sky at that time.

topic: How does a hydraulic lift lift a car?
hook: A mechanic pushes a small piston with one finger — and a car weighing 1.5 tonnes rises. Pascal explains the impossible.
think_question: Hydraulic systems power aircraft, diggers, and surgical robots. If hydraulic fluid could be replaced with something safer, what would you use?
q1_text: What scientific principle makes a hydraulic lift able to lift a heavy car?
q1_a: Pascal's law: pressure applied to a fluid is transmitted equally in all directions
q1_b: Bernoulli's principle: fast-moving fluid creates lift under the car
q1_c: Archimedes' principle: the oil displaces the car's weight upward
q2_text: Why is understanding Pascal's law more useful than just knowing hydraulics work?
q2_a: Knowing hydraulics work is sufficient for designing all mechanical systems
q2_b: It lets engineers calculate piston sizes needed to lift any given load
q2_c: Pascal's law only applies to water, not to the oil used in hydraulics
q3_text: If the output piston area of a hydraulic lift were doubled, what would you predict?
q3_a: The lift force would be halved because more area reduces the pressure
