q1_c: Self-sustainability in space means the habitat can operate for exactly one year before requiring a complete resupply mission.
q2_text: Why is understanding the mechanism of closed-loop life support more useful than knowing a habitat needs air and food?
q2_a: Space habitats are supplied continuously from Earth, so closed-loop systems are unnecessary to study.
q2_b: A mechanism explains the cause-and-effect chain and allows prediction in new situations.
q2_c: Oxygen in space can be captured directly from starlight, so understanding recycling is irrelevant.
q3_text: If the plant-growing system in a space habitat failed, what would you predict would happen to the crew over time?
q3_a: The crew would be unaffected because space habitats store enough packaged food for decades.
q3_b: The habitat's recycling system would automatically convert carbon dioxide back into food for the crew.
q3_c: The crew would face food shortages and rising carbon dioxide levels, as plants provide both food and oxygen recycling.

topic: Ultimate Challenge: Design a future sustainable city
hook: Future cities won't just be built for people — they'll be designed to have less impact than the wilderness they replaced.
think_question: If a sustainable city could be fully energy self-sufficient, what would it look like to the last resident who couldn't afford to live there?
q1_text: What is the central goal when designing a sustainable city?
q1_a: Meeting all human needs while minimising resource use and environmental impact
q1_b: Building as many tall buildings as possible to house the largest population
q1_c: Using the most advanced technology regardless of energy or material cost
q2_text: Why is a systems-thinking approach more useful than solving one problem at a time?
q2_a: Solving individual problems one by one is the most efficient design strategy
q2_b: Sustainable city systems are interconnected; fixing one part affects all others
q2_c: Systems thinking only applies to large cities with over one million residents
q3_text: If a sustainable city removed all cars and relied only on cycling and walking, what would you predict?
q3_a: Air pollution would increase because more people outdoors release more CO2
q3_b: Energy demand would increase because more lighting would be needed on paths
q3_c: Air quality and public health would improve and carbon emissions would drop

topic: Ultimate Challenge: Build a physics model explaining a real-world phenomenon
hook: A good physics model can predict the future — but how do you know when your model is actually correct and when it's just fitting noise?
think_question: Physics is full of models that worked perfectly until they didn't. How should scientists decide when to patch a model versus discard it entirely?
q1_text: What is the first step when building a scientific model to explain a real-world phenomenon?
q1_a: Identify and clearly describe the phenomenon you want to explain before introducing any theory
q1_b: Write the mathematical equations first, then find a phenomenon that matches the formula
q1_c: Search for an existing model online and apply it directly without any personalised adaptation
q2_text: Why is identifying the mechanism within a physics model more useful than just stating what happens?
q2_a: Stating what happens is sufficient for full marks in all Class 9 physics assessments
q2_b: A mechanism explains cause-and-effect and allows prediction in new situations
q2_c: Physics models are decorative tools that visualise results without needing explanatory depth
q3_text: If your physics model made a prediction that did not match experimental data, what should you do?
q3_a: Discard the experiment results because a well-built model is always more reliable than data
q3_b: Accept the mismatch as proof that the phenomenon is too complex for any scientific model
q3_c: Revise the model to account for the new evidence and test the updated prediction again

topic: Ultimate Challenge: Solve a real-world science problem using Class 10 concepts
hook: Real science doesn't come with textbook labels — the most powerful problems require mixing chemistry, biology, and physics at once.
think_question: If you had to use Class 10 concepts to design water purification for a remote village, what combination of principles would you apply?
q1_text: Which Class 10 concept best explains why a solar panel generates electricity from sunlight?
q1_a: Photoelectric effect: photons knock electrons free, creating current in the circuit
q1_b: Electromagnetic induction: sunlight spins a coil inside a magnetic field
q1_c: Chemical reactions: sunlight converts silicon into electrical charge carriers
q2_text: Why is applying multiple Class 10 concepts to a single real-world problem more powerful than one concept alone?
q2_a: Because real problems always have exactly one cause and one solution only
q2_b: Real systems involve overlapping mechanisms: combining concepts leads to deeper solutions
q2_c: Because Class 10 concepts are all identical and combining them changes nothing
q3_text: What would happen to electric power output of a solar panel on a cloudy day?
q3_a: Output would be identical because solar panels use reflected ground light not direct sunlight
q3_b: Output would increase because cloud cover reduces temperature and improves panel efficiency
q3_c: Output would decrease because fewer photons reach the panel to generate the photoelectric effect

topic: Research Challenge: Explain one major unanswered scientific question
hook: Science's most exciting questions are the ones with no answer yet. Pick any — and every year, a new tool might crack it open.
think_question: Choose one unanswered question in physics or biology. Describe what kind of experiment might resolve it within the next 20 years.
q1_text: Which of the following is a major genuinely unanswered question in modern science?
q1_a: The nature of dark matter and dark energy dominating the universe's mass-energy content
q1_b: Why does the Sun rise in the east, which scientists have not yet explained through observation?
q1_c: How does photosynthesis convert light into glucose, which remains completely unknown to biologists?
q2_text: Why is framing a research question around a mechanism more useful than simply identifying an unknown fact?
q2_a: Mechanism-based questions eliminate the need for experimental evidence in scientific research
q2_b: A mechanistic question identifies cause-and-effect relationships that guide productive investigation and testable hypotheses
q2_c: Unknown facts are more prestigious than mechanism questions in published scientific literature
q3_text: If a scientist proposes that dark matter consists of a new particle, what would the next scientific step be?
q3_a: Immediately accept the hypothesis because it is proposed by a credentialed scientist
q3_b: Reject the hypothesis because all subatomic particles were discovered in the 20th century
q3_c: Design experiments that could detect the proposed particle or rule out its properties through observation

topic: Grand Challenge: What will the next scientific revolution be?
hook: Every major revolution in science — from heliocentrism to quantum mechanics — seemed impossible until it suddenly seemed obvious.
think_question: If quantum mechanics and general relativity were successfully unified, which current technology would need to be completely redesigned?
q1_text: Which of the following best describes how major scientific revolutions occur historically?
q1_a: Anomalies accumulate until a new paradigm replaces the old framework entirely
q1_b: Scientists vote democratically to replace one theory with another by consensus
q1_c: Governments fund research that confirms existing theories and discards alternatives
q2_text: Why is unifying quantum mechanics with general relativity considered the biggest open challenge?
q2_a: Both theories are completely wrong and must be discarded before a new theory can emerge
q2_b: They describe the same phenomena at different scales and always produce identical predictions
q2_c: They use fundamentally incompatible mathematical frameworks that break down at extreme scales
q3_text: If a future theory successfully unifies quantum mechanics and gravity, what would it predict?
q3_a: That gravity does not actually exist and all attraction is caused by electromagnetic fields
q3_b: That atoms are made of four fundamental particles rather than the current three quark types
q3_c: Physics inside black holes and at the Big Bang singularity, which current theories cannot describe
